arXiv:2605.31381v1 [cs.CL] 29 May 2026

LLM Judges Inconsistently Disagree Across Safety Criteria and Harm Categories

Krishnapriya Vishnubhotla Affiliation: National Research Council, Canada    Soumya Vajjala Affiliation: National Research Council, Canada    Akriti Vij Affiliation: IMDA, Singapore Correspondence: krishnapriya.vishnubhotla@nrc-cnrc.gc.ca    Isar Nejadgholi Affiliation: National Research Council, Canada
Abstract

We evaluate the consistency of automated judges in conducting a multi-dimensional safety evaluation in a reference-free setup. Our results indicate that Large Language Models are unreliable judges in identifying safety issues related to machine-generated advice in regulated domains such as finance, although they are more reliable at identifying more overt forms of unsafe/harmful content such as violence. The degree of inconsistency in a model’s judgments can vary significantly by the chosen safety criteria and can be impacted by the language of the content and its linguistic style as well. Finally, there is high disagreement among different judges for the same output, across domains, safety criteria, and languages. These findings provide new insights on the practice of using LLMs as evaluators and offer several recommendations for practitioners on how to use automated judges in practical scenarios.

1 Introduction

Identifying unsafe content in Large Language Model (LLM) input/output has received much attention from the NLP research community in the recent past, and several taxonomies (Xie et al., 2025; Zeng et al., 2025) and datasets (Röttger et al., 2024; Cui et al., 2025) have been developed to evaluate LLM safety. The LLM-as-a-Judge paradigm has become a common means of evaluating the safety of LLMs (Wang et al., 2024, e.g.,) owing to the flexible nature of their specifications, although specialized fine-tuned classifiers for safety such as Granite Guardian (Padhi et al., 2025) and LlamaGuard (Inan et al., 2023) also exist. Safety evaluations typically view safety as a uni-dimensional safe vs unsafe construct. However, there may be multiple criteria to consider in real-world scenarios, such as whether an LLM is providing helpful output, if there are enough warnings issued, if there an outright refusal, etc. How do we understand the suitability of LLM judges when we consider such a multi-dimensional notion of safety? We address this question in this paper.

Much of the existing research on assessing AI safety tends to focus on queries or responses that cover obviously harmful content such as violence, hate speech, illegal activities, etc. There is some emerging work on evaluating LLMs for safety in other real-world scenarios, such as providing advice in regulated domains or in automated decision making based on user information (Zeng et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2025). In this paper, we compare LLM judges’ performance on both categories of queries with a multi-criteria definition of safety, and metrics that capture the self-consistency of a single judge and cross-consistency among multiple judges, which are described below:

  • •

    Self-consistency examines whether a judge is consistently giving the same evaluations for different semantically invariant transformations of given input, such as translations or paraphrases. This is important to understand the validity of LLM-as-a-Judge construct.

  • •

    Cross-consistency examines whether different judges consistently agree with each other given the same input. This is important to understand the validity of the practice of using LLMs-as-a-Jury (Verga et al., 2024), where a team of LLMs are employed to evaluate the output of a model.

We conduct this study in a reference free evaluation setup, i.e., where no gold standard output is assumed to be provided, reflecting the potential usage of LLM-as-a-Judge in real world safety evaluations. Our results indicate that LLMs are generally poor judges in identifying safety issues related to LLM generated advice in regulated domains such as finance, and are better at identifying more explicit forms of harmful content such as violence. Further, they are inconsistent in judging semantically-equivalent (i.e, translated and paraphrased) variations of a given response (low self-consistency), highlighting the potential for jailbreaking the judges through such text transformations. The same input when given to multiple judges also elicits contrasting judgments (low cross consistency), with varying degrees of disagreements across the different safety criteria.

Our main contributions are as follows:

  1. 1.

    We develop a workflow that allows for measuring consistency in LLM judgments across six different safety-related criteria in the absence of gold-standard annotations.

  2. 2.

    We evaluate self- and cross-consistency of judgments from six widely-used, state-of-the-art LLMs on a dataset of ≈350\approx 350 safety prompts, covering two types of risk categories and across 6 languages.

  3. 3.

    We identify key limitations in the use of raw agreement scores to measure consistency among judgments, and show the utility of chance-corrected agreement metrics in such contexts.

Our analyses highlight the limitations of using LLM judges in identifying potentially unsafe LLM generated content. While we focused on safety evaluations in this paper, the approach we followed can also inform practitioners on how to choose the right LLM judge (or a jury) for any given application scenario.

In the rest of the paper, we will situate our work in the context of other ongoing research on LLM judges (Section 2), explain our methodology in detail (Section 3), followed by a deeper discussion about our results (Section 4). Section 5 summarizes our key findings and outlines several best practices for practitioners.

2 Related Work

Large Language Models as evaluators have become increasingly common as a scalable alternative to human annotation across NLP tasks. While most contemporary research focuses on the accuracy of LLM judges compared to human annotators (Chiang and Lee, 2023; Tan et al., 2025; Bavaresco et al., 2025, e.g.,), a growing line of research challenges the assumption that LLMs are valid evaluation tools, looking at ways to measure the reliability of LLM judges (Feng et al., 2026; Dev et al., 2026), consistency across multiple runs (Haldar and Hockenmaier, 2025), different forms of bias (Zhou et al., 2026; Shi et al., 2025; Thakur et al., 2025), and reliance on superficial cues (Marioriyad et al., 2026). Strategies to mitigate such biases are also studied (Marioriyad et al., 2026). Chehbouni et al. (2025) go beyond analyzing the reliability of the LLM-as-a-judge setting, and questions the validity of this approach, highlighting the limitations of current evaluation practices for Natural Language Generation in general. Meta-analyses (Li et al., 2024), statistical frameworks (Dubois et al., 2025), and robustness evaluations under multilingual and multimodal settings (Fu and Liu, 2025; Padarha et al., ; Vij et al., 2026; Seah et al., 2026; Chung and Freienthal, 2026) also converge on the conclusion that current LLM judges operate as unstable measurement instruments for evaluating various criteria.

LLM Judges for Safety Evaluations: One aspect where the use of LLM judges specifically relates to this paper is in detecting harmful/unsafe content in LLM-generated output. Recent research has shown that LLM judges are not consistent in their safety judgments in the context of input artifacts such as apologetic or verbose phrasing (Chen and Goldfarb-Tarrant, 2025); others showed multilingual and dialect-level inconsistency in identifying toxic content (Aakanksha et al., 2024; Faisal et al., 2025). However, a majority of this work focuses on scenarios where gold standard reference outputs are available, and operationalizes safety as a uni-dimensional construct. Benchmarks like AIR-Bench (Zeng et al., 2025), AILuminate (Ghosh et al., 2025), and SorryBench (Xie et al., 2025) introduce new taxonomies of harm and address more open-ended, reference-free safety scenarios; however, they still focus exclusively on refusal as the desired response. As notions of safe behavior by LLMs become more nuanced (for example, moving from refusal to safe responses), safety needs to be operationalized as a multi-dimensional evaluation (Yuan et al., 2025) incorporating notions of helpfulness along with safety. In this paper, we build on existing research on automated safety evaluations for open ended scenarios, develop a multi-dimensional safety evaluation process, and compare various LLM judges both in terms of their self-consistency and cross-consistency.

3 Methodology

Our aim is to evaluate the (a) within-judge self-consistency, and (b) between-judge cross-consistency of LLM Judges in making safety judgments for semantically consistent transformations of response text. To study these, we designed a workflow shown in Figure 2, and explained below.

3.1 Seed Queries and Query Variation Generation

We took 50 seed queries from AIRBench-2024 (Zeng et al., 2025) from the two categories under “Operational Misuse” in their taxonomy- “Automated Decision Making”, and “Advice in Regulated Industries” (opmisuse). We also took 39 seed queries from the “Violence and Extremism/Child and Self-Harm/Political Usage/Criminal Activities” (violence) categories as representative queries for more unambiguous types of harm. For both categories, the queries contain details that can be termed culture/demographic based, but we expect the safety evaluations of the LLM generated outputs for these queries to be culture-agnostic.

We generated 5 variations for each of the 50 opmisuse seed queries by prompting GPT-4o-Mini to adapt the given input to different geographies and cultures by changing the names of people, places, currencies, etc., without actually answering the question (prompt in Figure A.1). This resulted in a total of 300 queries for this group (50 queries + 250 variations). We did a quick quality check to ensure the generated queries are indeed variations of the source query. For violence, this strategy did not work as the model refused to generate a variation in several cases. We therefore manually generated between 1-2 variations for each of the 39 queries, obtaining a total of 56 queries from this category. It is important to note that some query variations already exist in the original AIRBench, but we did not consider them as they only show stylistic variation without changing any information in the text such as names, locations and other details in the personal profile descriptions. Table A.1 in the Appendix shows the variations generated for a single source query as an example.

3.2 Response and Response Variation Generation

All the responses for both query categories were generated by prompting GPT-4o-Mini with default temperature settings. The choice of this model is motivated by its general popularity and cost efficiency. Since our goal is to evaluate the performance of LLMs as judges, we chose to use a single, strong, generator model. We then generated two kinds of semantically consistent variations for each model response:

  1. 1.

    Translations: All query-response pairs from opmisuse and violence were translated from English into five languages -- French, Arabic, Farsi, Telugu, and Hindi (chosen based on the availability of native speakers) using Google Translate11 1 https://translate.google.com/.

  2. 2.

    Paraphrases: For the opmisuse responses, which provided high variability, we designed an editing procedure that explicitly preserves the underlying semantic content while varying surface-level linguistic properties. Specifically, given an original query–response pair, we instructed the generator model to generate ten edited variants of the response (prompt provided in Appendix, Figure B.1). These include “evaluative strength” (stronger vs. weaker endorsement), “register” (formal vs. conversational tone), “discourse structure” (verdict-first vs. verdict-last organization), “explicitness of judgment” (implicit vs. explicit evaluation), and verbosity (compressed vs. expanded responses). We did not repeat this process for violence as the generator model predominantly produced refusals or standardized safety disclaimers, resulting in limited linguistic and structural diversity in responses.

Table 1 summarizes the query-response data used to evaluate the LLM judges in our experiments.

3.3 Judge Prompts and Models

We used two judge prompts - one focused on query safety and the other on response safety. For query safety evaluation, we designed a three level scoring schema (Figure C.1 in the Appendix) that identifies a query as one of safe, dual-use and unsafe, following Yuan et al. (2025). Our response safety evaluation prompt (Figure C.2 in the Appendix) takes a query-response pair as input and evaluates whether the model generated response is safe considering six safety dimensions with Yes/No responses for each. They are: Refusal (whether the model refuses to answer), Safety (Is the response safe?), Helpfulness (Is the response helpful?), Explanation (Is the model explaining its decision?), Warnings (Is the model issuing any warnings or disclaimers?), Cultural Sensitivity (Is the model considering the cultural cues from the prompt while responding?). For each of these dimensions, we prompt the judge to also offer a one-line explanation for its judgment. Figure C.3 in the appendix shows an example output from our LLM judge for response safety covering these six safety dimensions. We used six judge models: Gemini-2.5-Flash, GPT-4o-Mini, Claude-Haiku-4.5, Command-A, LLama-3.3-70B, and Gemma-3-27B. The choice of judges aimed to achieve a balance between open-weight and proprietary models, and ensuring a coverage of diverse model sizes.

3.4 Agreement Calculation

Since each judge in each setting acts as a safety annotator, we use established metrics of inter-annotator agreement to measure agreement between judges, and report Krippendorff’s Alpha (Hayes and Krippendorff, 2007) as a multi-annotator reliability measure. We also recorded the Pairwise Cohen’s Kappa (Cohen, 1960) for every pair of judges and the exact percentage agreement as an additional measure because chance-corrected metrics can be difficult to interpret under skewed label distributions, which are common in safety evaluation (e.g., near-universal “no” for refusal in some settings). In such cases, Krippendorff’s Alpha and Cohen’s Kappa may be deflated due to prevalence effects even when judges match frequently, or become unstable when one label dominates. Raw agreement provides an interpretable upper-level view of stability and helps distinguish genuinely inconsistent judging from metric artifacts caused by extreme class imbalance.

All LLMs both for generation and judging were accessed via a ReAct call from dspy22 2 https://dspy.ai/ to OpenRouter33 3 https://openrouter.ai/, keeping the default settings for temperature for all models.44 4 https://openrouter.ai/docs/api/reference/parameters We plan to share the source code and the all the subsequent data generated upon acceptance.

4 Results

We discuss our results considering four aspects: query safety, response safety, self-consistency and cross-consistency of LLM judges, followed by a short qualitative analysis.

4.1 Query Safety

We start with comparing the LLM judge assessment of query safety (prompted as shown in Figure C.1) with judgments from LlamaGuard4-12B (Inan et al., 2023), a safety fine-tuned classifier model (note that while LLamaGuard makes only a safe versus unsafe distinction, our LLM judge performs a three-way classification). Table 2 presents the results. We notice that most of the opmisuse queries are categorized as safe by both LLamaGuard and the LLM judges, compared to violence where all the LLM judges score <10%<10\% of the queries as safe. Among the judges, gemma-3-27b-it is an outlier in opmisuse and evaluates most queries as dual use, which is a reasonable judgment in advice-seeking scenarios. Similar results to English are observed when we translate the queries into different languages (See Table D.1 and Figure D.1 in the appendix for these details), with some difference in exact percentages numbers across languages, indicating that the safety fine-tuning that the models undergo may need to cover broader categories beyond explicitly harmful content.

4.2 Response Safety

Figure 3 shows a comparison of the safety evaluations of LLM judges using our 6-dimensional rubric (prompt in Figure C.2), for the English query-response pairs. We observe that the notion of “what is a safe response?” is neither uniform nor uni-dimensional. While all models are generally closer in their judgments of safety for the violence category, Haiku stands out compared to other LLM judges in opmisuse, identifying most responses as unsafe, and providing an explanation that it is not safe for an LLM to provide such advice in regulated domains. Similarly, Command-A judge tends to give a higher score for the question “Is the LLM response giving enough warnings?” compared to other judges in opmisuse. There are larger variations in the Cultural Sensitivity dimension across LLMs for the violence subset. All these point to strong disagreements among the judges in interpreting model responses, even within English, which is typically the language most LLMs are well-trained on. That leads us to the question of how these differences and disagreements manifest across semantically invariant transformations such as translations or paraphrases. We answer this question considering both the self-consistency of a judge across the response variations, as well as cross-consistency among the various judges for a given set of instances.

4.3 Self-Consistency of LLM Judges in Evaluating Response Safety

We evaluate the self-consistency of an LLM judge across semantically consistent variations i.e., translations and paraphrased variations generated as explained in Section 3. Table 3 reports Krippendorff’s α\alpha together with the percentage overlap for each safety dimension across six languages we considered (English + 5 translated versions), for all six judges. For Warnings, Explanations and Helpfulness, we generally observe high percentage overlap, but when corrected for chance, a​l​p​h​aalpha can range from low (e.g., Haiku for Explanation-violence ) to moderate (e.g., Gemma for Helpfulness-opmisuse ) to high (e.g, Command-A for Helpfulness-violence ). All models show more reliable agreement across languages on these criteria in the violence category compared to the opmisuse category. Note that only cases with high overlap percentage and high a​l​p​h​aalpha signal true reliability and consistency across languages.

For Refusal and Safety, high and reliable agreement is observed in the violence category for most judges, but often very low a​l​p​h​aalpha despite high percentage overlap in the opmisuse category. In such cases, the high raw agreement reflects label prevalence rather than genuine evaluation reliability. Within opmisuse, the most stable judgments occur for criteria tied to explicit textual cues such as Explanation, and Warnings. Cultural Sensitivity remains the least reliable dimension (only Haiku in opmisuse and Llama in violence show high reliability), suggesting that evaluating culturally grounded aspects of responses is highly sensitive to linguistic context for most of the LLM judges we employed in this study.

For the opmisuse category, we further study self-consistency by looking at whether the LLM judge reaches the same verdict across various (query, response) pairs where the query is the same and the responses are semantically consistent variations of the source response. Note that as described in Section 3, we could not generate such variations for violence. Table 4 summarizes the results.

The highest agreement for all judges is observed for the Refusal criterion, showing a moderate a​l​p​h​aalpha. Compared to the cross-lingual setting, paraphrased variations yield a more balanced label distribution, reducing dominance by a single class and resulting in more stable chance-corrected agreement estimates. For the Safety criterion, the percentage overlap between response variations is also very high across all judges, but the corresponding α\alpha values are substantially lower than Safety. For Explanations, Warnings and Refusal, there is low to moderate agreement across variations, though often lower than the cross-lingual self-consistency. Overall, across both kinds of semantically consistent variations (i.e., translations and response variations), we observe several inconsistencies for all judges, for most of the safety criteria. This calls for developing better calibration practices while choosing an LLM judge for safety evaluation.

4.4 Cross-Consistency among LLM Judges

Cross-consistency among judges within each language is shown in Table 5. In the opmisuse category, the Refusal criterion shows extremely high percentage agreement and moderate α\alpha values in all languages, with the exception of Telugu, followed by Explanation and Helpfulness. Warnings criterion exhibits a high percentage overlap across languages but relatively low α\alpha values. The weakest agreement across judges occurs for the Safety criterion. Despite moderate overlap values, the corresponding α\alpha values are near zero (and negative) across all languages. This suggests that safety judgments for opmisuse are highly subjective and sensitive to model-specific interpretation.

As expected, the cross-judge agreement is substantially higher for violence in comparison, with Refusal criterion having the strongest agreement, followed by a moderate-to-high cross-judge agreement for Safety and Helpfulness criteria, and moderate agreement for Warnings and Explanation criteria. The Cultural Sensitivity dimension exhibits the weakest cross-judge agreement in this category. Despite moderate overlap values, the corresponding α\alpha scores remain close to zero across languages, indicating that judges frequently disagree in their interpretation of culturally grounded aspects of responses.

Overall, the cross-consistency experiments indicate that the judges frequently disagree among themselves for making safety related decisions across languages, especially for opmisuse . Comparing pairwise agreement between judges may be useful in such cases to choose the LLM judges in a jury carefully for more consistent performance. Appendix E shows additional analysis comparing different judges in terms of the average pairwise agreement.

4.5 Qualitative Analysis

To understand the cross-lingual differences in judgments better, we manually analyzed a subset of the data, taking English and Hindi query-response pairs of the opmisuse category and Gemini-2.5-Flash’s judgments of both. Our qualitative observations focus on two aspects of the judge output: not acknowledging the lack of warnings and disclaimers, and inconsistent interpretation of the safety criteria.

Lack of warnings or disclaimers: We observed that the generator model often fails to generate disclaimers when dealing with topics such as credit score estimation, visa extension determination, hiring decision, etc., and delivers a declarative single sentence judgment (e.g., The predicted credit score range is 700-750). The judge model fails to acknowledge the lack of such warnings in the generated output, despite being prompted to do so. The judge also shows discrepancies in detecting the lack of such warnings between the two languages we analyzed. See the example in the Appendix Table F.1, where the judge labels the Hindi translated response as Unsafe for lack of warnings and the original English response as Safe despite that. In general, we observed that this judge is better at detecting appropriate content than identifying omitted criteria.

Inconsistent interpretation of criteria: We also observed that the same judge interprets subjective criteria such as Cultural Sensitivity and Explanation inconsistently across languages. Cultural Sensitivity may be interpreted along a spectrum ranging from the mere presence of cultural cues to indicators of discrimination or stereotyping. Similarly, Explanation is sometimes interpreted as the model providing reasoning for its answer, and at other times as supplying supporting evidence for its judgment. In several cases, violations of safety are mentioned under Helpfulness or Warnings, but the instance is still labeled as Safe.

Together with the quantitative analyses, these qualitative observations emphasize the limitations of using LLM judges in automated decision making scenarios, and call for further research into the development of best practices for employing such models as judges in the future.

5 Discussion

Our results provide a consistent picture of LLM judges as inconsistent measurement instruments. Across both self-consistency and cross-consistency analyses, we observe that agreement is not uniform across criteria and categories: dimensions tied to explicit and observable signals, such as Refusal in the violence category and, to a lesser extent, Explanation in both categories, exhibit relatively high and stable agreement across languages and across judges. In contrast, more interpretive dimensions such as Safety and especially Cultural Sensitivity in both categories, and Helpfulness in the opmisuse category, show substantially lower agreement, which indicates a greater sensitivity of these dimensions to model-specific interpretations and linguistic variation. The contrast between opmisuse and Violence indicates that calibrating the judges for the judgment context is essential. Our results also show that this inconsistency is highly impacted by the language and the linguistic form and style of the response, calling for more precise judge prompt design and model selection methodologies in multi-lingual and multi-cultural settings.

A key finding is the divergence between raw agreement and chance-corrected agreement. In several cases, particularly in the opmisuse category, we observe high percentage overlap alongside near-zero (or even negative) agreement coefficients. This pattern reflects strong label imbalance, where judges consistently assign the same dominant label (e.g., “safe”), leading to inflated raw agreement without meaningful reliability. This highlights an important methodological implication: relying solely on raw agreement can substantially overestimate the consistency of LLM judges, especially in settings where one class dominates. Instead, agreement metrics that account for chance, such as Krippendorff’s α\alpha or Cohen’s κ\kappa, are essential for correctly interpreting judge behavior.

Cross-judge disagreement remains substantial (Table 5) across languages, despite individual judges demonstrating reasonable self-consistency. This indicates that different LLMs do not share a common definition of safety. raising concerns about the validity of using multiple LLMs as a “jury” in a multilingual setting. Agreement across judges is particularly weak for dimensions such as Cultural Sensitivity, where interpretations vary not only across models but also across languages. Therefore, such criteria may be inherently underspecified or difficult to operationalize in a consistent manner. Also, a judge may stand out in terms of agreement with other judges, for some criteria. For example, Haiku shows the highest agreement with other judges for Explanations in the opmisuse category (See Table E.1). These observations call for further study on how to choose LLMs when making a jury. Cross-judge consistency on the measurement dimension could be considered as a criteria while choosing a jury of LLMs.

These findings have direct implications for the practical use of LLMs as evaluators. First, LLM judge based evaluation pipelines should carefully consider which dimensions are being measured, as not all criteria are equally reliable. Second, reporting both raw and chance-corrected agreement is critical to avoid misleading conclusions about consistency. Third, the use of multiple judges does not automatically guarantee reliability and may instead introduce additional variability if judges are not aligned. Finally, our results suggest that LLM-as-a-Judge may be more suitable for detecting clear, surface-level safety signals than for evaluating nuanced or context-dependent aspects of model behavior.

Limitations

We identify a few limitations in our approach, discussed below:

  • •

    Single generator model: All our experiments with LLM judges rely on a single generator model, which can be perceived as a limitation. However, our focus in this paper is on how various LLM judges react to the same input, and how a given LLM judge reacts to semantically invariant transformations of the same input. Thus, we focused on keeping one generator model, and experimenting with several judge models. We do not anticipate significant differences in the overall conclusions of these experiments because of a different generator model.

  • •

    Limited Variations to prompts and responses: Our prompt variation and the response variation processes explore a limited set of possibilities: replacing the geographical and cultural details in the prompts, and using translation and paraphrasing for response variation generation. The space of potential variations is unlimited, but these limited variations are still more scalable than human generated variations.

  • •

    opmisuse and violence Comparison: We compared advice in regulated domains to other forms of overt harmful content, but the number of samples are not equal for both the categories, owing to the difficulty in scaling variation generation for the violence subset. While this can be considered a potential limitation, the comparisons do give us consistent observations despite that sample size differences.

  • •

    No gold annotations: All the prompt/response variation procedures rely on automated methods and do not have a thorough human annotation. This is a potential limitation, but since our focus is on relative comparisons among the judges and their inconsistency for a given text, we see this as a part of the experimental design.

Appendix D Query Safety Evaluations

Detailed results for query safety evaluation across languages are shown in Table D.1, reporting the percentage of prompts labeled as safe and dual-use in each language. In the opmisuse category most instances are tagged as Safe by LllamaGaurd, with French queries being tagged as most safe (70.9%) while Hindi queries being tagged as least safe (30.43%). LLM judges are highly inconsistent with LlamaGaurd in terms of the proportion of queries being tagged as safe, with Gemma labeling most queries as dual-use across languages. For the violence category Telugu is tagged as least safe by LlamaGaurd (20.69%) and Arabic, Farsi and Hindi as most safe ( 37%). LLM judges are more cautious than LlamaGaurd in tagging this category as safe and tag some of them as dualuse but mostly as unsafe. Particularly Gemma tags none of the queries in this category as safe.

Figure D.1 shows the per-category (benign, dual-use and unsafe) categorization of LLM judges across languages of opmisuse and violence. Consistent with Table D.1, across languages, queries in the OpMisuse category are more frequently labeled as benign or dual-use, with relatively low proportions of unsafe classifications. In contrast, the Violence category is consistently dominated by unsafe labels across all judges and languages. While the overall patterns are broadly consistent across languages, there is noticeable variation across judges—particularly in the assignment of dual-use labels, which highlights differences in how borderline cases are interpreted.

Appendix E Cross-judge Consistency Analysis by Pairwise Agreement Scores

Cross-consistency of each judge with all other judges across evaluation criteria is quantified in Table E.1 as the average of pairwise Cohen Kappa agreement scores, and further illustrated in Figure E.1, which shows the distribution of these agreement scores across language pairs.

Operational Misuse:

inter-judge agreement is generally low across most criteria despite high overlap, indicating that agreement is often driven by dominant labels rather than consistent shared judgments. This is most evident for Safety (e.g., Gemma: κ=0.02\kappa=0.02 with 84.60%84.60\% overlap; GPT: κ=0.07\kappa=0.07 with 84.66%84.66\% overlap) and Cultural (GPT: κ=0.02\kappa=0.02, Gemini: κ=0.14\kappa=0.14), where κ\kappa remains low across judges. In contrast, Refusal shows moderate agreement (e.g., Llama: κ=0.56\kappa=0.56, Gemini: κ=0.51\kappa=0.51) with near-perfect overlap (∼99%\sim 99\%), suggesting more consistent alignment. Explanation exhibits relatively higher agreement compared to other criteria (e.g., Haiku: κ=0.66\kappa=0.66, GPT: κ=0.63\kappa=0.63), while Helpfulness remains low-to-moderate (κ≈0.23\kappa\approx 0.23–0.350.35) despite high overlap (∼91\sim 91–93%93\%). Notable deviations include Command-A’s low agreement for Warnings (κ=0.07\kappa=0.07, 58.93%58.93\% overlap), indicating substantial disagreement with other judges. Overall, agreement patterns in this category are dominated by label imbalance, limiting the interpretability of raw overlap. Also, Haiku stands out in this category with relatively low overlap in Safety (44.88%44.88\%), which reflects the fact that what is labeld as safe by other judges is frequently labeled as unsafe by Haiku.

Violence & Extremism:

inter-judge agreement is substantially higher and more meaningful across most criteria. Refusal shows the strongest and most consistent agreement (e.g., Llama: κ=0.93\kappa=0.93, Command-A: κ=0.91\kappa=0.91, Gemini/GPT: κ≈0.89\kappa\approx 0.89) with high overlap (∼95\sim 95–96%96\%). Helpfulness also exhibits strong alignment for most judges (Gemma: κ=0.84\kappa=0.84, Gemini: κ=0.83\kappa=0.83, GPT: κ=0.81\kappa=0.81), although Haiku deviates with lower agreement (κ=0.34\kappa=0.34, 69.34%69.34\% overlap). Safety and Explanation show moderate-to-high agreement (e.g., Gemma: κ=0.64\kappa=0.64 Safety, κ=0.70\kappa=0.70 Explanation), while Warnings remains more variable across judges (e.g., Command-A: κ=0.41\kappa=0.41 vs. GPT: κ=0.68\kappa=0.68). In contrast to other criteria, Cultural exhibits consistently low agreement across all judges (e.g., Gemini: κ=0.07\kappa=0.07, GPT: κ=0.14\kappa=0.14, Gemma: κ=−0.04\kappa=-0.04), along with lower overlap (∼52\sim 52–65%65\%), indicating substantial divergence in judgments. Overall, this category demonstrates stronger and more reliable inter-judge agreement, particularly for well-defined criteria, while subjective dimensions remain less stable.

Also, as shown in Figure E.1, for some criteria, a judge may stand out in terms of agreement with other judges, showing high average and low variation in its agreement degree. For example, Gemini shows the highest agreement with other judges for Warnings in the opmisuse category, with a small standard variation. As another example, Gemma is consistently in high agreement with other judges in terms of Helpfulness in the violence category. These observations can be used to select the right set of judges for a specific criterion.

Appendix F Qualitative Analysis - An Example

Table F.1 shows one example query that asks for a “creditworthiness” assessment of a candidate’s profile, where the generator model gives a one-sentence output with a predicted credit score. In this case, while the judge model scored the English output as Safe, it scored the translated Hindi version as Unsafe. Human annotator agrees with the judgment generated for Hindi, in this case – in several instances dealing with topics such as credit score estimation, visa extension determination, hiring decision, etc., the judge model fails to acknowledge the lack of warnings or disclaimers in the generated output, despite being prompted to do so.
